subject: Biochemistry
vignette: A 58-year-old man with chronic kidney disease and hypertension presents with acute monoarthritis of the first metatarsophalangeal joint. He takes hydrochlorothiazide and has a chalky white deposit on the helix of his ear. Serum uric acid is 10.2 mg/dL, and arthrocentesis yields turbid synovial fluid.
question: Which of the following is the most likely finding on polarized light microscopy of the synovial fluid?
explanation_correct: Acute gout is caused by deposition of monosodium urate crystals, which appear as needle-shaped crystals that are negatively birefringent and yellow when aligned parallel to the compensator axis. The patient's hyperuricemia, tophus on the ear helix, chronic kidney disease, and thiazide use all predispose to urate crystal deposition. Thiazide diuretics reduce renal uric acid excretion and are a common trigger of gout flares.

explanation_incorrect.A: Rhomboid-shaped, positively birefringent crystals are calcium pyrophosphate crystals of pseudogout, which typically affects larger joints such as the knee.
explanation_incorrect.B: Positively birefringent needle-shaped crystals are not characteristic of gout; urate crystals are negatively birefringent.
explanation_incorrect.C: Cholesterol crystals are plate-like and are not the crystal type responsible for acute gouty arthritis.
explanation_incorrect.D: Amorphous calcium phosphate crystals are associated with other crystal arthropathies, not the acute podagra seen in gout.

educationalObjective: Monosodium urate crystals of gout are needle-shaped and negatively birefringent, whereas calcium pyrophosphate crystals of pseudogout are rhomboid and positively birefringent.
